input.question: Which educational institution did Willy Schwabacher attend?

documents.text: As Willy Schwabacher delved deeper into the world of numismatics, his fascination with the intricacies of coin design and the stories they told only grew stronger. It was during his undergraduate years at the University of Nottingham, surrounded by the historic architecture and vibrant cultural scene of the East Midlands, that his passion truly began to take shape. Willy would often spend hours pouring over dusty tomes in the university's sprawling library, uncovering hidden gems and obscure references that shed new light on his research. His favorite haunt was the George Green Library, where the musty scent of old books and the soft hum of fluorescent lights created the perfect atmosphere for immersion. It was there, nestled between shelves stacked high with volumes on art history and archaeology, that he stumbled upon an obscure treatise on medieval coinage. The author, a little-known scholar named Dr. Emilia Fothergill, had a way of bringing the past to life with her vivid descriptions of 12th-century minting techniques and the rivalries between royal courts. Willy was captivated by her writing style, which seemed to dance across the page like the intricate patterns on a Byzantine solidus. He devoured the entire book in a single sitting, his mind racing with the possibilities of how he could apply Dr. Fothergill's theories to his own research. As the semester drew to a close, Willy decided to take a chance and reach out to Dr. Fothergill, hoping to discuss her work and perhaps even secure an introduction to the academic community. To his surprise, she responded promptly, inviting him to meet at the university's Department of Archaeology, where she was scheduled to deliver a guest lecture on the numismatic significance of the Crusades. The day of the lecture arrived, and Willy made his way to the department, his heart racing with excitement. As he entered the crowded seminar room, he spotted Dr. Fothergill, a statuesque woman with silver hair and piercing green eyes, standing at the podium. Her words were like a symphony, weaving together threads of history, politics, and art to create a rich tapestry that left the audience entranced. After the lecture, Willy mustered the courage to approach Dr. Fothergill, introducing himself and sharing his own research on the coinage of the Holy Roman Empire. To his delight, she was impressed by his knowledge and enthusiasm, offering words of encouragement and a valuable connection to the academic community.
